questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=1$ for  $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =1\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y-x,\,x+y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=2$ for  $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y-x,\,x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,y-x,\,x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x+y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(x+y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}+y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\,y+\frac{1}{2}\,{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,xz,\,z+{y}^{2}⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,xz,\,z+{y}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,xz,\,z+{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})+0-(z+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}-z}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{{x}^{2}-z}{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-z\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y,\,z+3⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x+y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{3}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,z+3⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x,\,y,\,x+y+3⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-x-y+(x+y+3)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨y,\,z,\,2x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,z,\,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨y,\,2,\,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot {[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$
